samples.question: This page shows one small near-black stamp built from square blocks, together with red, blue, green, orange, grey and purple decorations that lie elsewhere on the open page. Only the near-black stamp ink decides the answer; the coloured decorations never count, even when a decoration is drawn as a closed ring or frame with its own pale middle. Pale channels cut the stamp into separate pieces. A piece is a maximal patch of near-black ink whose blocks are joined edge to edge; blocks that meet only at a corner are not joined, and the stamp is drawn so that this case never arises. A hole is a patch of pale paper that lies wholly inside the ink, so that no pale route leads from it out to the open page around the stamp; pale paper that reaches the open page through a channel is not a hole, however deep it cuts. Every hole belongs to the one piece that rings it. The question is about how the holes are shared out among the pieces, not about how many there are of either: at most one piece is ever left bare, and the same numbers of pieces and of holes occur with both answers. How many pieces the stamp has, how many holes it shuts in, where the stamp sits on the page, how large its blocks are, how much ink it carries and which colours appear never decide the answer by themselves. Does every piece of the stamp shut in at least one hole of its own? Answer yes or no.
